work.text: Ōkyo painted these panoramas in the summer of 1784. Regarded as Kyoto's most important painting teacher and accomplished artist, he had studied Western painting techniques, "realistic" sketching from nature, and traditional Japanese style painting (yamato-e). The naturalistic quality of these scenes results from a blend of detailed observation of nature and a remote, even detached regard for man's place in the world.

moment.text: Landscape for him became a new spacing, trees a new law of growth ; angles supplanted curves everywhere ; textures were studied as never before … In this way Okio actually forestalled the work of the Barbizon school of France

source.author: Ernest F. Fenollosa
source.title: Epochs of Chinese and Japanese Art, Vol. II

moment.text: Its primary patrons were rich merchants in and around Kyoto/Osaka and also appealed to the kamigata who were of the established aristocrat and artisan families of the Imperial capital during the late 18th/19th centuries.
moment.lead: Of the school that grew from Ōkyo's studio:

matters.text: For Okio made a specialty of the scenery of the neighbourhoods, the flora and fauna dear to his locality.
